questions.stem: Which is an example of natural change to Earth's systems rather than human-induced change?
options: glacial and interglacial cycles over a million years
the rise in carbon dioxide since the Industrial Revolution
the conversion of lowland rainforest into oil palm estates
the spread of cities onto coastal wetlands and floodplains
questions.explanation: Glacial cycles are paced by changes in Earth's orbit and amplified by natural feedbacks. Rising carbon dioxide, plantation expansion and urban growth are driven by people.

questions.stem: Compared with most natural changes to Earth's systems in the past, current human-induced changes are distinctive mainly because of their:
options: slow rate and local extent
regular cycle of about 100 000 years
complete reversibility within a year
rapid rate and global extent
questions.explanation: Natural changes such as glacial cycles usually unfold over thousands of years. Human-induced warming, land clearing and biodiversity loss are happening over decades to centuries and across the whole planet.

questions.stem: Some scientists use the term 'Anthropocene' for the present. The idea behind the term is that:
options: the Earth has entered a new ice age caused by volcanic activity
human populations are now declining in every part of the world
human activity now dominates many of Earth's systems
natural processes have stopped operating anywhere on the planet
questions.explanation: The Anthropocene concept recognises that people now shape the climate, land cover, oceans and biodiversity at a planetary scale. Natural processes continue, but human influence is profound.

questions.stem: A river delta is shrinking. Which evidence would best show that the change is mainly human-induced rather than natural?
options: the delta is made of fine sediment that rivers carried from distant mountains
upstream dams that trap sediment were built just before shrinking began
the delta has grown and shrunk many times over the last ten thousand years
the delta lies in a region with a highly seasonal monsoon rainfall pattern
questions.explanation: A change that begins when a human activity starts, and has a clear mechanism (dams cutting sediment supply), points to human causes. Long-term natural fluctuations alone would not explain the timing.

questions.stem: According to the IPCC's Sixth Assessment Report, global surface temperature in 2011-2020 was higher than in 1850-1900 by about:
questions.explanation: The IPCC found warming of about 1.1 °C over that period, with land warming faster than the ocean. This may seem small, but it is a global average with large effects on extremes.

questions.stem: Measurements of atmospheric carbon dioxide at Mauna Loa in Hawaii, begun in 1958, show:
options: a rise until 1980, then a fall to pre-industrial levels
a steady rise each year, with a small seasonal cycle
a steady fall each year, with no seasonal variation
no change in concentration since the 1950s
questions.explanation: The Keeling Curve rises every year because of human emissions, with a small annual wiggle as Northern Hemisphere plants take up carbon in summer and release it in winter.

questions.stem: Which observation is direct evidence of climate change in the contemporary world?
options: a volcanic eruption that darkened the sky for a week
a one-off flood in a single river catchment
glaciers retreating on every continent that has them
a cold winter recorded at a single weather station
questions.explanation: Climate change is shown by long-term, widespread trends such as glacier retreat, rising sea level and warming temperatures. A single cold winter or flood is weather, not a climate trend.

questions.stem: Global mean sea level has risen by about 20 cm since 1900. Which two processes are the main causes?
options: sinking of the ocean floor and evaporation from the oceans
increased rainfall over the oceans and erosion of coastlines
thermal expansion of warming sea water and melting land ice
melting of floating sea ice and increased river flow to the sea
questions.explanation: Water expands as it warms, and melting glaciers and ice sheets add water to the ocean. Floating sea ice already displaces its own weight of water, so its melting adds very little.

questions.stem: Satellite records since 1979 show that Arctic sea ice in late summer has:
options: grown steadily in extent
stayed exactly the same
disappeared completely every year
declined markedly in extent
questions.explanation: The September minimum extent of Arctic sea ice has fallen sharply since satellite records began, one of the clearest indicators of warming. The Arctic still has sea ice at its summer minimum.

questions.stem: A table shows a town's annual mean temperature anomalies: 1990s average +0.2 °C, 2000s +0.4 °C, 2010s +0.7 °C. Which conclusion is best supported?
options: the warming is caused only by the town's urban growth
the town has a warming trend of about 0.25 °C per decade
the town will be exactly 1.2 °C warmer in the 2030s
each individual year in the 2010s was hotter than 1990
questions.explanation: The anomaly rose 0.5 °C over two decades, an average of 0.25 °C per decade. Decade averages do not show that every year was warmer, cannot predict an exact future value, and do not identify the cause.

questions.stem: Air trapped in Antarctic ice cores shows that over the past 800 000 years:
options: temperature stayed constant while carbon dioxide varied
carbon dioxide was always far higher than it is today
carbon dioxide and temperature rose and fell together
carbon dioxide stayed constant while temperature varied
questions.explanation: Ice cores show carbon dioxide closely tracking glacial and interglacial temperatures. Today's concentration, above 400 ppm, is far higher than at any time in that record, which stayed below about 300 ppm.

questions.stem: Which evidence best shows that the recent rise in atmospheric carbon dioxide comes mainly from burning fossil fuels?
options: carbon dioxide has risen most during years of high solar activity
ocean water has become less acidic as carbon dioxide has risen
the added carbon has the isotope signature of ancient plants
carbon dioxide levels are highest directly above active volcanoes
questions.explanation: Fossil fuels formed from ancient plants are depleted in carbon-13 and contain no carbon-14, and the atmosphere shows exactly this change. Volcanoes emit far less carbon dioxide than people, and the oceans are becoming more acidic.

questions.stem: Solar output has not increased since the 1950s, yet global temperatures have risen strongly. What does this suggest?
options: global temperatures are not really rising
solar output and temperature are always unrelated
changes in the sun cannot explain recent warming
the sun is the main cause of recent warming
questions.explanation: If the sun were driving recent warming, solar output would have risen too. Its flat or slightly falling trend points to other causes, mainly rising greenhouse gases.

questions.stem: The 1991 eruption of Mount Pinatubo in the Philippines cooled global temperatures for about a year or two. This happened because:
options: sulfur aerosols in the stratosphere reflected sunlight
the eruption released large amounts of carbon dioxide
lava flows covered large areas of tropical forest
the eruption moved the Earth further from the sun
questions.explanation: Large eruptions inject sulfur dioxide that forms reflective aerosols high in the atmosphere, causing short-term cooling. The effect fades as the aerosols settle out, so volcanoes cannot explain long-term warming.

questions.stem: Which of these is a 'proxy' record used to reconstruct past climates before instruments existed?
options: weather balloons
thermometers
tree rings
satellite images
questions.explanation: Proxies such as tree rings, ice cores, corals, pollen and sediment layers preserve indirect evidence of past climate. Satellites, balloons and thermometers measure climate directly but only for recent times.

questions.stem: Climate models reproduce observed warming since 1950 only when human greenhouse gas emissions are included alongside natural factors. This is evidence that:
options: natural factors alone fully explain recent warming
climate models cannot reproduce any past climate
greenhouse gases have a cooling effect on climate
human influence is the main cause of recent warming
questions.explanation: Attribution studies compare simulations with and without human influences. Natural factors alone would have produced little warming since 1950, so the observed rise is attributed mainly to human activity.

questions.stem: In recent decades, most global deforestation has taken place in:
options: Western Europe
Antarctica
the tropics
the Arctic tundra
questions.explanation: Tropical forests in South America, Africa and South-East Asia account for most forest loss, mainly from clearing for agriculture. Forest area in many temperate countries is stable or growing.

questions.stem: Under the UN Convention to Combat Desertification, desertification is land degradation in dry areas resulting from:
options: climatic variations and human activities
the natural spread of existing deserts only
sea level rise flooding coastal farmland
glaciers advancing over arid grasslands
questions.explanation: Desertification affects arid, semi-arid and dry sub-humid lands and is caused by a combination of drought and human pressures such as overgrazing, clearing and poor irrigation. It is not just deserts expanding.

questions.stem: The Sahel, on the southern edge of the Sahara, suffered severe droughts and land degradation in the 1970s and 1980s. Which combination best explains the degradation?
options: drought plus overgrazing and clearing for fuel
heavy rainfall combined with rapid glacier advance
volcanic eruptions combined with rising sea level
cold winters combined with too few grazing animals
questions.explanation: Lower rainfall, rising populations, more livestock and cutting of trees for firewood removed vegetation and exposed soils. Rainfall has partly recovered since, showing the role of climate variability.

questions.stem: Which statement best describes the global pattern of mountain glaciers since the late 1800s?
options: most have advanced steadily as the climate cooled
only tropical glaciers have changed in size
glaciers have stayed the same size everywhere
most have retreated, faster in recent decades
questions.explanation: Glaciers worldwide have lost mass, with faster loss in recent decades. A few have advanced locally, but the global trend is clearly one of retreat.

questions.stem: The Greenland and Antarctic ice sheets are both losing mass. Why does this matter beyond the polar regions?
options: melting ice sheets add salt, making oceans more saline
melting land ice raises sea level, threatening coasts
melting ice sheets lower sea level, exposing new farmland
ice sheet loss has no effect outside the polar regions
questions.explanation: Water from land ice flows into the ocean and raises sea level, affecting low-lying coasts and islands worldwide. Fresh meltwater actually lowers salinity locally and can affect ocean circulation.

questions.stem: FAO forest assessments show that, at the global scale since the 1990s, net forest area has:
options: risen sharply as deforestation stopped in the tropics
stayed exactly the same in every region of the world
fallen faster each decade, with no regrowth anywhere
kept falling, though the rate of net loss has slowed
questions.explanation: Net loss continues because tropical clearing outweighs forest gains elsewhere, but the net rate fell between the 1990s and 2010s as some countries expanded forest through planting and regrowth.

questions.stem: Methane from cattle and flooded rice paddies is a significant greenhouse gas. This shows that land use contributes to climate change through:
options: the cooling effect of crops on the lower atmosphere
the removal of carbon dioxide by grazing animals
the reflection of sunlight by flooded rice paddies
emissions from agriculture as well as from clearing
questions.explanation: Agriculture emits methane from livestock digestion and waterlogged rice fields and nitrous oxide from fertilisers, adding to the carbon dioxide released when forests are cleared.

questions.stem: Borneo, the island with some of the world's most biodiverse rainforest, is shared by which countries?
options: Malaysia, the Philippines and Laos
Papua New Guinea, Indonesia and Timor-Leste
Indonesia, Malaysia and Brunei
Indonesia, Thailand and Vietnam
questions.explanation: Borneo is divided between Indonesia (Kalimantan), Malaysia (Sabah and Sarawak) and Brunei. New Guinea is the island shared by Indonesia and Papua New Guinea.

questions.stem: Which land use change has been a leading driver of rainforest loss in Borneo since the 1990s?
options: flooding of forest by rising sea level
expansion of oil palm plantations
growth of ski resorts in the uplands
conversion of forest to wheat farms
questions.explanation: Large areas of logged and intact forest have been converted to oil palm and pulpwood plantations. Indonesia and Malaysia produce most of the world's palm oil. Logging, fires and mining also contribute.

questions.stem: Satellite images of Borneo from 1990 and 2020 are compared to study rainforest loss. Which aspect of the change can they best measure?
options: the views of local communities about plantation jobs
the extent and rate of forest loss across the island
the number of orangutans living in each forest patch
the price received by farmers for each tonne of palm oil
questions.explanation: Repeated satellite images allow forest area to be mapped at each date, so the extent and annual rate of loss can be calculated. Animal counts, prices and views need field surveys and other data.

questions.stem: A district in Borneo had 5 000 km² of forest in 2000 and 3 800 km² in 2020. What was the average annual rate of loss as a share of the 2000 area?
options: 0.6% per year
12% per year
1.2% per year
24% per year
questions.explanation: The loss is 1 200 km² over 20 years, or 60 km² per year. As a share of 5 000 km², 60 / 5 000 = 1.2% per year. 24% is the total loss over the whole period.

questions.stem: When rainforest is cleared for plantations, how does this interrupt the hydrological system?
options: no change, because plantations use water exactly as rainforest does
rainfall stops completely over the cleared area within a year
less interception and transpiration, so more runoff and flooding
more interception and transpiration, so less runoff and erosion
questions.explanation: Rainforest intercepts rain and returns large amounts of water to the air by transpiration. Clearing increases runoff, erosion and flood peaks, and can reduce local rainfall over large areas.

questions.stem: Many plantations in Borneo have been developed on drained peat swamp forest. Why does this land use change affect the climate system so strongly?
options: peat contains no carbon, so its loss only affects biodiversity
drained peat oxidises and burns, releasing stored carbon
peat swamps absorb more carbon once they are drained and planted
draining peat raises the water table and cools the atmosphere
questions.explanation: Peat stores carbon built up over thousands of years. Drainage lets it decompose and makes it highly flammable, so peat fires, as in 1997 and 2015, release vast amounts of carbon dioxide and smoke.

questions.stem: Smoke haze from peat and forest fires in Indonesia in 2015 affected neighbouring countries such as Singapore and Malaysia. This shows that impacts of land cover change occur:
options: only in the year that the forest is first cleared
at a range of scales, local to regional and global
only at the local scale where clearing takes place
only at the global scale, never in nearby places
questions.explanation: Fires harmed local health and livelihoods, haze crossed borders at the regional scale, and emissions added to global climate change. Impacts can also persist for years after clearing.

questions.stem: Rainforest loss in Borneo has contributed to the decline of the Bornean orangutan, now listed as Critically Endangered. This is mainly because:
options: plantations provide more food than the original rainforest
orangutans prefer open land and leave intact forest
rising sea level has flooded all of its habitat
its forest habitat has been lost and broken into fragments
questions.explanation: Clearing, fragmentation, fires and associated hunting reduce and isolate populations. Orangutans depend on large areas of forest for food and nesting.

questions.stem: Which statement best evaluates the impacts of oil palm expansion in Borneo?
options: it brings jobs but causes biodiversity loss and emissions
it has only positive impacts because palm oil is a renewable crop
it has no economic benefits because palm oil has no export markets
it improves biodiversity because plantations hold more species
questions.explanation: Plantations provide export earnings, jobs and income for smallholders, but replacing rainforest and peat reduces biodiversity, releases carbon and can cause conflicts over land. Plantations support far fewer species than rainforest.

questions.stem: Indonesia placed a moratorium on new licences to clear primary forest and peatland, and in 2019 made it permanent. This response operates at which scale?
options: national
local
global
household
questions.explanation: A government policy covering the whole country is a national-scale response. Certification schemes such as the Roundtable on Sustainable Palm Oil work through global markets.

questions.stem: The Roundtable on Sustainable Palm Oil (RSPO) certifies palm oil produced under standards that include no clearing of primary forest. Which is a limitation of this response?
options: it requires all oil palm to be grown outside the tropics
it is voluntary, and certified oil is only part of world supply
it bans the sale of all palm oil in every country of the world
it is run by a single national government with strict laws
questions.explanation: Certification depends on companies choosing to join and buyers paying for certified oil, and enforcement relies on audits. Much palm oil is still uncertified.

questions.stem: Rainforest loss reduces the carbon stored in vegetation and soils. How does this link land cover change to climate change?
options: clearing absorbs carbon dioxide from the atmosphere
clearing has no effect on greenhouse gases
clearing lowers temperatures by increasing cloud cover
clearing emits carbon dioxide and removes a sink
questions.explanation: Burning and decay of cleared vegetation emit carbon dioxide, and the lost forest can no longer absorb carbon as it grows. Land use change is a significant source of global emissions.

questions.stem: Which is the strongest evidence that rainforest loss in Borneo is human-induced rather than natural?
options: cleared areas match the boundaries of plantation licences
the island has a hot, wet equatorial climate year-round
rainforest has covered Borneo for millions of years
Borneo has some of the world's highest rainfall totals
questions.explanation: When forest loss lines up with the straight boundaries of plantation concessions and roads on satellite images, the cause is clearly human land use. Climate and long forest history do not explain recent loss.
